summary: `runBackendCli` installs the stdin-EOF shutdown listeners AFTER `createStdioBridge` has already put `process.stdin` into flowing mode, so an EOF that arrives during attach is emitted with nobody listening and is never re-delivered. This is the exact orphan `installShutdown`'s own doc says the stdin events exist to catch: "an orphaned bridge (parent crashed or SIGKILLed) gets EOF and no signal, so without them it heart-beats a ghost peer into every peer's roster".
failure: Launch any backend bin whose parent is already gone (or simply `parley-redis --config x.yaml < /dev/null`) with the README's recommended `live_push: { enabled: true }`. Ordering: `createStdioBridge` → `bridge.attach` → `server.connect(transport)` → SDK `StdioServerTransport.start()` attaches `stdin.on('data')` (flowing mode; the SDK never listens for 'end' or 'close' — node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/server/stdio.js:30-31) → `await startPushLoop(...)` awaits `plugin.subscribe()`, which is real network I/O for every network backend (bridge-redis/src/index.ts:265 `await this.connectReader(reader)`) → only then does `runBackendCli` call `installShutdown`. Reproduced standalone: with one macrotask in that window `process.stdin.readableEnded === true` and neither the 'end' nor the 'close' listener ever fires (`fired=[]`); with the listeners registered before the await, `fired=["end"]`. Wrong output: `bridge.shutdown()` never runs — no presence `goodbye`, no `plugin.disconnect()`, no `server.close()`; for a socket-holding backend the process never exits and heartbeats a ghost peer into every peer's `parley_list_users` roster.
remediation: Arm the guard against the state, not only the event: after registering the listeners in `installShutdown`, synchronously check whether EOF has already happened. Widen `ShutdownHost['stdin']` to `{ on(...): unknown; readableEnded?: boolean }` and append `if (host.stdin.readableEnded === true) shutdown();` after the two `stdin.on` calls. The existing `shuttingDown` latch makes the check idempotent against a later real 'end'. (Re-ordering `installShutdown` before `createStdioBridge` is not sufficient on its own and is awkward, because the teardown closure needs a bridge that does not exist yet.)
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a lifecycle listener armed after its event can still be missed", not this one call site. Replace `cli/shutdown.test.ts`'s stub-host table (which by construction can never observe ordering — every trigger fires after `installShutdown` returns) with a parameterized case over a REAL `Readable`: for each of {already ended before install, ends during install, ends after install} × {0, 1, 2 macrotasks of delay between putting the stream in flowing mode and calling `installShutdown`}, assert `onShutdown` ran exactly once. Add a matching row for a stream `destroy()`ed without an 'end'. The existing `SEQUENCES` table is too narrow to have caught this because it fires every trigger through an EventEmitter the test itself controls, after registration.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Node's `stream.Readable.prototype.readableEnded`, true once 'end' has been emitted — verified in the repro (`readableEnded= true fired= []`). Also relies on the existing branch `if (shuttingDown) return;` in `installShutdown`, so the added call cannot double-tear-down when a real 'end' follows.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no argv or config that is rejected today becomes accepted.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A bridge started with stdin already at EOF now tears down immediately instead of serving. `parley-sqlite --config x.yaml < /dev/null`, which today runs indefinitely, would exit at once. That is the intended semantics for a stdio MCP server (no parent, no client) but it IS a visible behaviour change for anyone smoke-testing a bin that way.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the patch to the real tree and ran `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core packages/conformance`: 62 files / 3784 tests passed. I looked specifically at `cli/shutdown.test.ts` (its `wire()` passes a bare `EventEmitter` as `stdin`, so `readableEnded` is `undefined` and the strict `=== true` never fires — all 12 sequences unaffected), `transport/root-lifecycle.test.ts` and `transport/root-teardown-bounds.test.ts` (neither goes through `installShutdown`).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the reported case rather than hiding it: the whole defect is that EOF already happened, and `readableEnded` is precisely that state. What would still be broken: a stdin `destroy()`ed without ever emitting 'end' leaves `readableEnded === false`, so that path stays uncovered; adding `|| host.stdin.destroyed === true` would cover it but risks firing on an unrelated destroy, so it needs its own decision.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two orderings matter. (a) EOF before `installShutdown`: listeners are registered, then the synchronous `readableEnded` check fires `shutdown()` once; the latch is set, so nothing else can run it. (b) EOF after `installShutdown`: the check sees `false`, the 'end' listener fires later and runs `shutdown()` once. Two callers on the new path: a SIGTERM racing the synchronous check — there is no await between registration and the check, so a signal handler cannot interleave before it; whichever lands first sets `shuttingDown` and the other returns immediately. No new suspension point is introduced.

summary: Both the operator-facing README and the `post_topics` field doc promise that a pattern widens post/fetch to any FULLY-MATCHING topic, with no mention of the 64-character `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` ceiling `Allowlist.has` actually enforces. The config loader accepts topics up to 512 characters (`beatString`), so the disagreeing region is reachable by an ordinary deployment. `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` is not exported from the barrel either, so a consumer has no way to name the limit the docs omit.
failure: `parseConfig({ identity: { handle: 'h' }, topics: ['ctx-demo'], post_topics: ['ops-.*'] })` loads clean. `allowlistFor(cfg).has('ops-' + 'a'.repeat(61))` (a 65-character topic that fully matches `ops-.*`) returns `false`, and `assert` throws `topic not allowed: "ops-aaa…" — post_topics patterns are only matched against topics of at most 64 characters (this one is 65); list it in `topics` instead`. The same 65-character string is accepted verbatim in `topics:` by the loader. README lines 62-63 (`post_topics: ["ops-.*"]  # optional: WIDENS post/fetch to any fully-matching topic`) and README's "Every topic argument goes through the topic `Allowlist`, which accepts a topic listed in `config.topics` **or** one fully matching a `post_topics` pattern" are both false in that region, as is `Allowlist`'s own class doc ("the EXPLICIT list PLUS any `post_topics` pattern match") and `AllowlistOptions.postPatterns`'s doc, which names the count cap and the ReDoS screen but not the input clamp.
remediation: State the ceiling everywhere the widening is promised: the `post_topics` field doc in config.ts, the `Allowlist` class doc and `AllowlistOptions.postPatterns` in allowlist.ts, and the README's `post_topics` comment and Allowlist paragraph — 'a pattern is only matched against topics of at most 64 characters; list a longer topic in `topics`'. Export `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` from index.ts so the number a consumer must respect is nameable rather than hardcoded. Do not raise the clamp: mutating it away made the suite hang in catastrophic backtracking, so it is load-bearing.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "every capability the core README promises is executed against the code", which is the gap that let this ship: `bridge-sqlite`, `bridge-redis` and `bridge-postgres` each ship a readme-truth suite and `@sharptrick/parley-core` — the package whose README IS the public API doc — ships none. Add `packages/bridge-core/src/readme-truth.test.ts` that extracts the README's config sample and its Allowlist paragraph and executes them, parameterized over topic lengths derived from `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` ({4, MAX-1, MAX, MAX+1, MAX_TOPIC_LEN}) crossed with the README's own `post_topics` example, asserting the README states whichever verdict the code gives at each length. `allowlist.test.ts`'s MATCH_ROWS already grades the clamp correctly but derives its expectation from `MAX_MATCH_INPUT`, so it can never notice that no prose anywhere mentions it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `Allowlist.has`'s `if (topic.length > MAX_MATCH_INPUT) return false;` (allowlist.ts:119) and `assert`'s `overLong` branch, which already produce the correct runtime message; the fix touches only prose plus one added `export` in index.ts.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the doc fix changes no behaviour. Exporting `MAX_MATCH_INPUT` adds a symbol to the public surface (a `feat:`-level, non-breaking addition).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.

summary: `stated-bounds.test.ts` derives its capacity rows by scanning `CAPACITY_MODULES`, a hard-coded array of four filenames. Its own doc says "The modules are scanned, so a capacity added to any of them needs a row here rather than arriving unpinned" — but 'any of them' is a literal list, so a capacity declared anywhere else in `src/` is never pinned. CLAUDE.md names this shape explicitly: "Prefer, always: a glob over `src/**` rather than one file path."
failure: Add `export const MAX_MENTION_LEN = 99;` to `packages/bridge-core/src/mentions.ts` (a src module not in `CAPACITY_MODULES`). Wrong output: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core packages/conformance` → 62 files / 3784 tests PASS. The 'has a row for every capacity the governed modules export' case never sees it, so a new operator-facing capacity — or an existing one relocated into a new file during a split — ships with its VALUE unpinned, which is exactly the failure the surrounding comment ("with every probe built as `'a'.repeat(bound - 1)`, `MAX_GLOB_LEN = 8` keeps the whole suite green") exists to prevent.

Add a `declared.length` floor derived from the walk (as `source-hygiene.test.ts` does with its 'reaches every workspace package, at every depth' case) so a broken walk cannot go green by finding nothing.

Parameterize the discovery: assert the walk reaches every directory under `src/` that contains a non-test `.ts` file (derived from the tree, not listed), and add a positive control that plants a temp file exporting a `MAX_*` constant in a scratch tree and asserts the extractor reports it. remediationCheck.reliesOn: `readFileSync` + the existing `/^export const ((?:MAX|MIN|DEFAULT)_[A-Z0-9_]+)\b/gm` regex, and `readdirSync(..., { recursive: true })` as `index.test.ts:15` already uses within this same package.

Each needs a `Capacity` row with a literal `expected` and a realistic input before the suite is green again — that work IS the fix, but it is not a one-line change. summary: The shared front-door fixture's teardown abandons every remaining resource on the first failure — the exact shape `buildBridge`'s `releaseAll` was hardened against ("Keep every step ATTEMPTED even after an earlier one rejects, so a backend whose close handshake fails cannot leave the transport connected and the process unable to exit"). The fixture that grades the doors does not follow the rule the doors follow.
failure: `closeFrontDoors()` is `for (const { server } of booted.values()) await server.close();` then `booted.clear()`, `const fx = await fixtures`, `await fx.idp.close()`, `await fx.plugin.disconnect()`. If the first of the four cached servers rejects on close (an in-flight request, a hung keep-alive socket), the other three stay listening, `booted` is never cleared, the FakeOidc express server is never closed and the FakePlugin is never disconnected. `auth/error-surface.test.ts` registers it as `afterAll(closeFrontDoors)`, so the outcome is a vitest worker with four live listeners and open handles — a hang or a forced teardown rather than one clear red assertion. The same class again in `appFor`: if `door.boot(port, fx)` or `app.server.listen(port)` rejects, the partially-booted server is never cached and never closed, so its socket leaks with no reference left to close it; and `fixturesUp`'s `fixtures ??= (async () => …)()` caches a REJECTED promise permanently, after which both every `appFor` and `closeFrontDoors` itself reject on `await fixtures` before closing anything.
remediation: Mirror `stdio-bridge.ts`'s `releaseAll`: in `closeFrontDoors`, wrap each `server.close()`, `idp.close()` and `plugin.disconnect()` in a try that collects failures, clear `booted` and reset `fixtures` in a `finally`, and rethrow an `AggregateError` at the end so a real close failure still reddens. In `appFor`, close the server in a catch before rethrowing. In `fixturesUp`, clear `fixtures` on rejection so a transient IdP-bind failure does not poison every later call.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "teardown stops at the first failure" wherever this package composes a release. Parameterize a case over the release points (`buildBridge.releaseAll`, `closeFrontDoors`, `remoteHttpApp.teardown` in testing/http-app.ts) × the position of the failing step (first, middle, last), injecting a rejecting close and asserting every OTHER step still ran and the failure surfaced. `transport/root-teardown-bounds.test.ts` grades the bridge's release under a hostile `post` but nothing grades the fixture's own, and a fixture that leaks turns a red into a hang, which is strictly worse to diagnose.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The already-shipped pattern in `packages/bridge-core/src/transport/stdio-bridge.ts:97-112` (`const attempt = async (step) => { try { await step(); } catch (e) { failures.push(e); } }` plus the `AggregateError` rethrow) — copied rather than invented.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A `closeFrontDoors()` in which some steps failed now still completes the rest before throwing, so a suite whose teardown previously hung can now finish and report.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: An `AggregateError` instead of the single underlying error, so any caller matching on the error's message or type would need updating. No current caller does — `afterAll(closeFrontDoors)` just awaits it.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped every importer of `front-doors.js` (`auth/error-surface.test.ts` and `transport/front-doors.test.ts`); neither asserts on what `closeFrontDoors` throws, and `transport/front-doors.test.ts` does not call it at all. I did not apply this remediation, so this is read off the call sites rather than run.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the surrounding habit remains, it fixes the fixture's own teardown but not the general rule — `testing/http-app.ts`'s `teardown` has the same shape (`await app.close(); await plugin.disconnect();`) and would still drop the plugin disconnect if the app close rejects. That is why the testUpgrade parameterizes over all three release points rather than pinning this one.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The orderings that matter are step-position: failure at the first, a middle and the last resource, each of which must leave the others released. Two callers on the new path: `closeFrontDoors` is registered once per file as `afterAll`, but `booted`/`fixtures` are module-level, so two test files in the same worker could both invoke it — the `finally` that clears `booted` and resets `fixtures` makes the second call a no-op rather than a double-close, which the current code (clearing only on the success path) does not guarantee.

Excluding `src/testing/**` from tsconfig also removes it from `tsc -b`'s type-checking of the src project, so those fixtures would be type-checked only by `tsconfig.test.json` — verify that project still includes them, or the exclude silently drops them from CI's type gate.

summary: An attacker-controlled presence page can exhaust filterReachable's 50 ms per-direction pattern allowance, after which every remaining peer is reported unreachable — and parley_list_users still answers `truncated: false`, so the agent is told an empty or gutted roster is the whole bus.
failure: Post 120 presence beats (handles hostile-0..119, each with 64 DISTINCT screen-safe sources of the shape `('[a-z]?' x16) + 'Z<n>'`, all fresher than the victim), plus one legitimate beat from `colleague` with `postTopics: ['ctx-.*']`, while the caller subscribes to a 60-char `ctx-aaa…` topic. Reproduced in-tree: `filterReachable(roster, {canPostTo: () => false, mySubscribedTopics: [MINE]})` spent 50.7 ms and returned `[]` — `colleague` is genuinely reachable (its pattern full-matches my subscribed topic) but is dropped because `budget()` returned undefined for every entry after the allowance ran out. list-users-tool.ts:132 then computes `truncated = (121 >= 500) || (121 >= 128) || (0 < 0)` = false, so the tool answers `{ users: [], truncated: false }` — indistinguishable from "nobody is on the bus". The suite's nearest case, presence.test.ts:753 'a hostile page cannot starve the other direction of its budget', builds the hostile page with `patterns: 0`, so it only exercises CROSS-direction starvation; and presence.test.ts:736 deliberately places the benign `partner` FIRST 'so the verdict is the predicate's and not the budget's'. Same-direction exhaustion is untested.
remediation: Make the exhaustion observable instead of silent. Add an optional `onAllowanceSpent?: () => void` to `filterReachable`'s opts, have `budget()` invoke it the first time it returns undefined (both the peerReach allowance and the budgeted(canPostTo) one), and OR the resulting flag into list-users-tool.ts's `truncated`. That discloses, but does not restore reach; the durable fix is to stop letting an attacker-chosen ENTRY COUNT consume a whole-call allowance — give each roster entry its own small allowance so one hostile entry cannot spend a later entry's, or evaluate patterns only for entries not already admitted by an explicit topic.
testUpgrade: Class: "an untrusted count silently switches a caller-facing predicate off, and the answer does not say so." Add a parameterized table over (which direction the hostile page inflates: peer-postTopics-inbound | peer-topics-outbound | both) x (where the benign peer sits in recency order: first | middle | LAST) x (how it is reachable: explicit shared topic | pattern-only), asserting for every cell that the benign peer is either still returned OR the result is flagged truncated — never dropped silently. The existing presence.test.ts:753 case is exactly one cell of that table (inflate outbound, benign last, pattern-only) and cannot see the same-direction diagonal. Pair it with a generator that emits N distinct screen-safe-but-costly sources so widening PATTERN_BUDGET_MS or MAX_RECORD_TOPICS re-derives the pressure rather than hard-coding it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `budget()`'s `if (spentMs >= PATTERN_BUDGET_MS) return undefined;` branch in presence-reach.ts:42 — the single place exhaustion is currently detectable — and list-users-tool.ts:132 `truncated: truncated || roster.length >= MAX_ROSTER_ENTRIES || capped.length < users.length`, which I would extend with a fourth disjunct.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the callback changes no filtering decision, so every input filtered today is filtered identically.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked the four rows of list-users-tool.test.ts 'every cause of a truncated roster is disclosed, and only when it applies' (the scanned presence history was full / the roster hit its entry cap / `limit` trimmed it / none of them): none of those pages carry costly patterns, so the new flag stays false and the 'only when it applies' row still passes. summary: MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS — the control the code itself says stops a far-future beat reading as "permanently live" and pinning a phantom peer at the top of the roster — is graded only by probes derived from its own value, so its value is free to move in the dangerous direction under a fully green suite.

A hostile beat with `at = now + 2 years` is then accepted by decodePresence, `nowMs - at` is hugely negative so `nowMs - at < ttlMs` holds forever, the peer is `online: true` immune to `online_only` and `since_ms`, and `lastSeenMs` sorts it first in every roster for two years. The two tests that look like they guard this — presence.test.ts:370-371 'exactly at the skew tolerance' / 'one ms beyond' — probe at `MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS` and `MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS + 1`, both derived from the constant, so they move with it. stated-bounds.test.ts is the file that exists to stop exactly this ('with every probe built as `'a'.repeat(bound - 1)`, `MAX_GLOB_LEN = 8` keeps the whole suite green'), and its own comment claims 'The modules are scanned, so a capacity added to any of them needs a row here rather than arriving unpinned' — but CAPACITY_MODULES at stated-bounds.test.ts:186 is the hardcoded list ['config.ts','identity-filter.ts','regex-safety.ts','topic-name.ts'], resolved relative to src/, which cannot see src/engine/ or src/transport/ at all. Thirteen capacities live there unregistered. I probed five of the others (MAX_ROSTER_ENTRIES, DEFAULT_ROSTER_LIMIT, MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES, MAX_FETCH_LIMIT) and each happened to be caught incidentally by a byte-budget or count assertion; MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS is the one with no such accident, because time has no byte cost.
remediation: Replace CAPACITY_MODULES' hardcoded file list with a recursive walk of `src/**/*.ts` excluding `*.test.ts` and `testing/`, and add a CAPACITIES row for every capacity the widened scan turns up — starting with MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS pinned to the literal 300_000 and paired with a realistic accepted input (a beat 30 s in the future decodes; one 6 min in the future does not).

summary: defaultReadStatePath documents its default as `${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}` — shell `:-`, which means "unset OR EMPTY" and is also what the XDG spec mandates — but implements it with `??`, which only covers unset. An empty XDG_STATE_HOME yields a RELATIVE state path under the process's cwd.

Consequence: the bridge started from a different directory finds no cursor, `catchUpTopic` takes the COLD START branch, and on-start catch-up re-drains and re-warms from the recent window instead of resuming — silently, with no error and no log. read-state.test.ts:123 and :192 set XDG_STATE_HOME to a mkdtemp path and the surrounding restore at :112-115 only distinguishes undefined; no case sets it to ''.

Consider additionally refusing a base that `isAbsolute()` says is relative, since the spec requires an absolute path and a relative one reintroduces the cwd coupling by another route.

I grepped the whole repo for XDG_STATE_HOME and found no test that sets it to ''.

summary: `assertTrustProxy` early-returns for every value that is neither a string nor an array, so Express's *function* form of `trust proxy` — which Express fully supports and which `() => true` spells identically to the boolean `true` the guard refuses by name — passes the guard untouched. The guard's own JSDoc claims the opposite: "The refusal is a property of what the value TRUSTS, not of how it is written."
failure: `createOAuthRemoteApp(plugin, cfg, { issuerUrl, verifyOwner, trustProxy: () => true })` boots healthy. Reproduced: `assertTrustProxy(() => true, 'trustProxy')` returns without throwing, while `assertTrustProxy(true, ...)` and `assertTrustProxy(['0.0.0.0/1','128.0.0.0/1'], ...)` both throw. Express then compiles that function straight into `trust proxy fn`, so `req.ip` is the leftmost `X-Forwarded-For` element the caller wrote, and every `/parley/consent` bucket (10 per 15 min) is minted fresh per forged header value — unlimited anonymous guesses at the owner passphrase, which is the exact exposure the guard exists to close.
remediation: Include functions in the probed set: `if (typeof value !== 'string' && !Array.isArray(value) && typeof value !== 'function') return;`. Express's `compileTrust` returns a function value verbatim as `trust proxy fn`, so the existing ADDRESS_SPACE probe grades it unchanged — verified: `()=>true` is flagged, `(ip)=>ip.startsWith('10.')` is accepted. One extra edit is required: `unboundedTrust` renders the value with `JSON.stringify`, which yields `undefined` for a function, producing the message "trustProxy must not be undefined"; render with `String(value)` (or a `typeof`-aware label) so the operator sees what they wrote.
testUpgrade: The class is "a value that trusts the whole address space, in a spelling the table's TYPE cannot hold". `WHOLE_SPACE_SPELLINGS` in remote.test.ts and `LEGITIMATE_PROXY_LISTS` in invariants.test.ts both declare `trustProxy: boolean | number | string | string[]`, which structurally excludes the function form — widen both to `unknown` (the guard's own parameter type) and add rows for `() => true`, `(ip: string) => ip.startsWith('10.')` (must be ACCEPTED), `new String('true')`, and `Object.assign(() => true, {})`. Better still, drive the refusal table from a generator over every form Express's `compileTrust` accepts (boolean, number, string, string[], function) so a spelling Express learns about later is graded the day it lands.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Express 5 `application.js`: `this.set('trust proxy', val)` sets `'trust proxy fn'` to `compileTrust(val)`, and `compileTrust` returns `val` unchanged when `typeof val === 'function'`. I traced this by running `express().set('trust proxy', ()=>true); app.get('trust proxy fn')('1.2.3.4', 0)` and observing `true`, and the discriminating case `(ip)=>ip.startsWith('10.')` observing `false`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no value accepted today becomes accepted that was not already
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `trustProxy: () => true` (and any function whose predicate returns true for all 256 IPv4 and 16 IPv6 probe addresses). A function that names real proxies, e.g. `(ip) => ip.startsWith('10.')`, is still accepted.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the one-line fix and ran the full auth suite: 15 files / 1057 tests, all green. I looked for callers passing a function in packages/, examples/ and docs/ (grep for `trustProxy`) — every call site passes a string, number, boolean or string[].
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It closes the function spelling only. Two acknowledged residues remain and are unaffected: a hop COUNT larger than the real chain (`trustProxy: 2`) still lets the caller write `req.ip` — remote.test.ts states this as `keyedOn: 'forged'` — and a partial cover such as `['0.0.0.0/1']` is still accepted by design (invariants.test.ts lists it as legitimate).

summary: `issue()` emits `scope: scopes.join(' ')` unconditionally, so a grant with no scopes produces `"scope": ""` in the RFC 6749 §5.1 token response. RFC 6749's ABNF is `scope = scope-token *( SP scope-token )` with `scope-token = 1*NQCHAR`; the empty string is not a valid `scope` value. The package already states this rule against itself in grant-params.ts:9-11 ("RFC 6749 §3.3 spells a scope token `1*NQCHAR`: an empty one never names one") and filters empty tokens out of the REQUEST, then re-introduces one in the RESPONSE.
failure: Reproduced end to end through the provider's public API: `authorize(client, { redirectUri, codeChallenge })` with no `scopes`, then `completeConsent`, then `exchangeAuthorizationCode` returns `{"access_token":"…","token_type":"bearer","expires_in":3600,"refresh_token":"…","scope":""}`. `exchangeRefreshToken` on that token returns `"scope": ""` too. Claude's connector requests no scopes, so this is the default response shape a strict client sees.
remediation: In `issue()`, spread the field conditionally: `...(scopes.length > 0 ? { scope: scopes.join(' ') } : {})`. RFC 6749 §5.1 makes `scope` OPTIONAL when it is identical to what the client requested — with nothing requested and nothing granted, omission is the conformant answer.
testUpgrade: The class is "a degenerate scope token crosses the wire in either direction". remote.test.ts's `SCOPE_REQUESTS` table already parameterizes the request side; extend each row with an `expectedResponseScope: string | undefined` column and assert the RAW `tokens.scope` against it rather than through `scopeSet()`, which normalizes `''`, `undefined` and `'mcp  mcp'` into the same set and therefore cannot see the response spelling at all. Add a row asserting that when `granted` is empty the field is ABSENT, and reuse the same column at both /authorize and the refresh grant so the two paths cannot drift.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `OAuthTokens` in @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/shared/auth.js declares `scope: z.string().optional()`, so omitting the key still parses; the SDK's token handler serializes whatever object the provider returns.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — this is a response-shaping change, no input validation moves
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: remote.test.ts "a degenerate scope token is dropped…" rows `an empty scope parameter` and `a lone space`, at BOTH /authorize and the refresh grant (4 cases). Their helper is `scopeSet = (s) => new Set(String(s).split(' ').filter(Boolean))`; with the field omitted, `String(undefined)` is `'undefined'`, so the set becomes `{'undefined'}` and no longer equals `new Set([])`. The helper must be fixed to handle absence (`s === undefined ? new Set() : …`) as part of the change. I verified this by mutating `issue()` to drop the field entirely, which turned 24 tests red across 2 files — that mutation is broader than the fix, but those 4 rows are among them.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken; the scope-narrowing logic on the refresh grant is untouched, since it reads `rec.scopes` (the array), never the serialized string.

The second call re-sets `env` (idempotent) and registers a second terminal error handler that can never run, because the first one terminates the response without calling `next`.

If a future refactor moves `hardenErrorSurface` OUT of `createRemoteHttpApp`, deleting these calls would leave the front doors unhardened — which is precisely why the fix should be paired with the router-stack assertion in testUpgrade rather than done alone.

summary: `rememberClient`'s `?? this.clients.keys().next().value` fallback carries a load-bearing JSDoc claim — "Keep the fall back to the oldest entry, so that a map full of owner-approved registrations cannot make a FRESH owner approval the one that fails" — and no test grades it.

With it deleted, `evictable` is `undefined`, the `if (evictable !== undefined)` guard skips the delete, and `this.clients.set(...)` runs anyway — so the MAX_CLIENTS=100 bound silently stops holding on the approval path. Either the documented lockout or the unbounded-growth regression can be introduced without the suite noticing.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none

summary: `DiscoveryDocumentSchema`'s trailing `.extend(OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema.shape)` exists to satisfy a stated invariant — "Keep the OIDC shape WINNING on shared keys, so that widening the mirror cannot tighten what a legitimate IdP is allowed to publish" — and nothing grades it.

I checked why: the two SDK schemas share 13 keys and, at @modelcontextprotocol/sdk's current version, none of them differ in optionality, so the precedence has no observable effect today. The day the SDK tightens one shared key on the OAuth side, a legitimate Keycloak realm would fail discovery at boot and the suite would still be green — and a refactor reordering the extends would land unnoticed.

Add a property assertion driven off the two SDK schemas rather than a fixture: for every key in `OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema.shape`, assert that `DiscoveryDocumentSchema.shape[key]` is the same schema object (reference equality is enough, and it fails loudly if the extends are reordered). Pair it with a round-trip: any document `OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema.parse` accepts, `DiscoveryDocumentSchema.parse` must also accept.

Write the guard against the DEPENDENCY, not a fixture: iterate `Object.keys(OpenIdProviderDiscoveryMetadataSchema.shape)` and assert both (a) precedence by identity and (b) that the RFC 8414-only keys `revocation_endpoint` and `introspection_endpoint` survive a parse. remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none. oidc-discovery.test.ts already asserts that `revocation_endpoint`/`introspection_endpoint` survive (dropping the OAuth extend turns 1 test red), so the added assertion complements rather than contradicts it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: No defect exists today; this makes a currently-invisible invariant observable. If the SDK never diverges, the assertion never fires — that is the point.

summary: `WHOLE_SPACE_SPELLINGS` opens with the right lesson — "A guard that enumerates SPELLINGS is a guard the next spelling walks past" — and then types its own subject field `type TrustProxy = boolean | number | string | string[]`, which structurally cannot hold the next spelling. `LEGITIMATE_PROXY_LISTS` in invariants.test.ts is narrower still (`string | string[]`). The tables also cannot express `new String('true')` or a wrapper object.

That reaches spellings nobody typed, which is exactly what the existing table's own header says it is trying to do.

No currently-passing row changes verdict: I re-ran the suite with finding 1's production fix applied and all 1057 tests stayed green, so every existing row keeps its answer under the widened guard.

summary: openDriver's `onDisk` heuristic exempts any path starting with `file::memory:` from the 0600 pre-creation and the -wal/-shm narrowing, but neither shipped driver enables SQLITE_OPEN_URI - so such a path is a literal filename and a real, world-readable on-disk store.
failure: backend_config `db_path: "file::memory:?cache=shared"` (the SQLite-documented shared in-memory URI) with umask 022. Reproduced: the cwd gains `file::memory:?cache=shared`, `...-wal` and `...-shm`, every one at mode 0644 - the whole conversation store and its WAL readable by every account on the host, with no stderr line. `precreate` and `restrictMode` are both skipped because `onDisk` is false; `synchronous = NORMAL` and the WAL read-back gate are skipped for the same reason, so the connection is also served without the mode check the README says is enforced.
remediation: Delete the `&& !path.startsWith('file::memory:')` term - neither better-sqlite3 nor node:sqlite honours URI filenames, so every path other than the exact string ':memory:' is on disk and must be hardened. Additionally reject a `db_path` beginning with `file:` in validateBackendConfig, so an operator who meant a URI gets a startup error naming the key rather than a file literally named after their URI.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the at-rest matrix in test/at-rest-mode.test.ts over a PATHS dimension rather than the single 'p.db' literal: ['p.db', 'file::memory:?cache=shared', 'file::memory:', 'file:p.db?mode=ro', 'p.db?x=1']. The invariant is 'if openDriver caused a file to appear at this path, that file and its sidecars are 0600' - derive the expectation from `existsSync` after the open, not from a hand-listed on-disk/in-memory split, so any future path form the heuristic mis-classifies is graded by construction. The existing matrix cannot catch this class because it hard-codes one filename.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `precreate` in at-rest.ts (`closeSync(openSync(path, 'a', 0o600))`, whose catch is silent so a genuinely-unopenable path still surfaces the driver's own error) and `restrictMode`'s `catch { return; }` for a sidecar that does not exist yet. It also relies on applyPragmas' `if (!onDisk) return;` branch no longer being taken for these paths, which means `journal_mode` must read back 'wal' - my probe printed `journal_mode {"journal_mode":"wal"}` for exactly this path, so the newly-reached gate passes.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: with the config guard, `db_path: "file:..."` now fails connect() instead of silently creating a file with that name. With the onDisk change alone, a `file::memory:*` path on a filesystem where the WAL conversion cannot be honoured is now refused rather than served - the same treatment every other on-disk path already gets.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found - I grepped src/ and test/ and README.md for `file::memory`, and it occurs on exactly one line, driver.ts:99. The `:memory:` cases in src/driver.test.ts ('skips :memory: without throwing', and the `onDisk:false` row of the OPENS table) use the bare `:memory:` string, which this fix leaves on the not-on-disk arm.

summary: The poll loop's teardown test re-reads mutable plugin state (`this.stopped`, `this.driver`), so a `connect()` re-entered from inside a handler re-satisfies it mid-tick and the loop resumes against the NEW store carrying the OLD store's lastSeen and storeId - invisible in subscriptionHealth() and absent from `cancellers`.
failure: An embedder does exactly what the README prescribes ("re-pointing an embedded plugin means disconnect() first") from inside a subscribe handler: `void p.disconnect(); void p.connect({db_path: B})`. Reproduced against store A (rowids 1-6) then store B: store B's rows b0..b5 are silently never delivered because the loop resumed at rowid 6 from store A; rows b6..b9 ARE delivered, carrying cursors `0fb147203501c37c.7`..`.10` while store B's own id is `14ba7544b74667fa` - cursors store B's own resumeAfter will classify as foreign and replay. Meanwhile `subscriptionHealth()` returns `[]` and `cancellers.length` is 0, so a supervisor sees no loop at all and nothing can stop it until the next disconnect(). The very comments in index.ts ("a second connect() would orphan every running poll loop", "a reconnect onto a different or reset store cannot resume a live loop at a rowid belonging to the previous one") name this outcome as the thing being prevented.
remediation: Add a generation counter owned by the lifecycle: increment it in both `connect()` and `disconnect()`, capture it in `subscribe()` alongside `storeId`, and return from `tick` whenever it differs from the current one. That makes the loop's identity, not the plugin's current state, decide whether the tick belongs.
testUpgrade: Extend test/lifecycle.test.ts's 'a teardown started from inside a handler' block into a table over the re-entrant ACTION rather than only `disconnect`: ['disconnect', 'disconnect twice', 'disconnect then connect to the same store', 'disconnect then connect to another store', 'connect without disconnect']. Assert the same observable pair for every row - after the batch, no further content reaches the handler, and every cursor the handler ever received carries the store id of the store that was connected when subscribe() ran. Keying on the cursor PREFIX (not just delivery count) is what makes a resumed cross-store loop visible; the existing rows only count rows and so cannot see it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `SqliteStore.tornDown()` (`return this.stopped || this.driver === undefined;`) - the fix adds a per-loop generation check beside it rather than replacing it, so the existing teardown behaviour is untouched; and `index.ts` connect()'s `this.stopped = false` / `this.health.length = 0` block, which is where the counter must be bumped for the new check to fire.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a poll tick belonging to a previous connect() generation, which today is accepted and reschedules itself.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found - I read test/lifecycle.test.ts's ORDERS table (its 'connect, subscribe, disconnect, connect again' row already declares loopDelivers:false) and its 'a reconnect reports nothing from the previous generation until it subscribes again' case, and test/catchup-live-handoff.test.ts's 'every reconnect cycle re-closes the window' (each cycle calls subscribe() again after connect(), so its loops are always current-generation). No test in the package expects a loop armed before a reconnect to keep delivering after it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Making connect() throw when `health.length > 0`, or clearing cancellers more aggressively, hides the symptom while the bug remains: the tick already in flight still finishes its in-memory batch against the new store's statements and still mints cursors under the old store id, because nothing in either change is read by the running tick.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The only interleaving is synchronous re-entry - connect() and disconnect() have no await before their state writes - so the ordering is tick -> handler -> disconnect -> connect -> tick resumes. Two callers on the new path: (a) an embedder calling disconnect()/connect() from outside, between two ticks: the generation is bumped with no tick in flight, and the loop's timer was already cleared by disconnect(), so behaviour is unchanged; (b) a handler doing it re-entrantly: the loop returns at its next per-row check and never reschedules. Neither leaves a pending timer, because disconnect() clears the canceller list before connect() re-arms.

summary: The 'Cross-process safety' section claims every connection opens with WAL + busy_timeout + synchronous=NORMAL and that a connection which did not reach WAL is refused rather than served. For `db_path: ":memory:"` - a configuration the README's own config table documents as supported - none of that holds.

An operator reading 'A connection that did not reach WAL is refused, not served' and configuring `:memory:` for a single-session deployment is told the process would have failed; it did not.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found - test/readme-claims.test.ts's rows for this section match on /journal_mode/, /readers never block the writer/i, /busy_timeout/, /retries instead of erroring/i and /lost on power loss/i, none of which a carve-out sentence removes.

summary: This package ships two drivers and says so in its own docblocks ('the driver is a DIMENSION of this file rather than an ambient fact'), but only test/conformance.test.ts and test/driver-parity.test.ts apply it. The other 15 test files construct SqlitePlugin directly and therefore grade better-sqlite3 twice.

That guards the class - 'a behaviour graded on one of two shipped configurations' - rather than the bigint bind instance.

summary: entryTimestamp's range clamp is `ms >= 0 && ms <= MAX_DATE_MS`, but the RangeError it exists to prevent only occurs at |ms| > 8.64e15. Every representable PRE-EPOCH instant a foreign writer puts in `ts` is silently rewritten to 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z. The JSDoc directly above claims "The entry's own `ts` when it is a real date" — 1969-07-20T20:17:40.000Z is a real date, and the code does not honour it.
failure: Reproduced against a live Redis: `XADD parley:moon * sender nasa content 'eagle has landed' ts 1969-07-20T20:17:40.000Z`, then `fetchRecent({topic:'moon'})` -> Message.timestamp === '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' instead of '1969-07-20T20:17:40.000Z'. Same on the subscribe path, since both go through rowToMessage. The whole package suite (798 tests) stays green.
remediation: Widen the lower bound to the symmetric one the ECMAScript Date range actually has: `new Date(ms >= -MAX_DATE_MS && ms <= MAX_DATE_MS ? ms : 0).toISOString()`. The upper bound stays as-is; the id-derived branch (`Number(id.split('-')[0])`) is non-negative by construction and is unaffected.
testUpgrade: The class is "a clamp whose accepted range is narrower than the range it is protecting". live-stream.test.ts's foreignEntries table is the right home, but every one of its from-ts rows is post-epoch, so it cannot see this. Widen it into a generated axis over Date's OWN bounds rather than hand-picked instants: derive rows from [-MAX_DATE_MS, -MAX_DATE_MS+1, -1, 0, 1, MAX_DATE_MS-1, MAX_DATE_MS] plus [-MAX_DATE_MS-1, MAX_DATE_MS+1] (the two that must fall back), each asserted as new Date(ms).toISOString() for the in-range ones and as the fallback for the out-of-range ones — so the boundary is graded from both sides and a future clamp change cannot narrow the range invisibly. The same generator should be applied to the id-derived branch, whose ms component is a uint64.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `new Date(ms).toISOString()` in entry.ts, which is well-defined for the whole closed interval [-8.64e15, 8.64e15] and throws RangeError only outside it; and MAX_DATE_MS = 8_640_000_000_000_000, which is already the exact bound.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An entry written with ts '1969-07-20T20:17:40.000Z' now normalizes to '1969-07-20T20:17:40.000Z' instead of '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the out-of-range fallback to new Date(0) is unchanged for anything past |8.64e15|.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied this exact edit and re-ran the whole bridge-redis suite against a live server: 798/798 still pass. I looked specifically at live-stream.test.ts's foreignEntries (WELL_KNOWN_TS 2020-05-06, '2020-05-06T07:08:09+02:00', '2020-05-06', 'Tue, 05 Nov 2024', 'Mon Jan 01 2020', '12/25/2021', '2020') and at idRows (all ids derived from 2n**53n / LAST_DATE_MS / ID_CEILING, all non-negative) — every row is at or after the epoch, so none of them is on this branch.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes. If it were applied and the bug somehow remained, the only thing still broken would be the same silent rewrite; nothing is hidden, because the clamp's fallback path is still reachable and still asserted for the out-of-range ids.

summary: assertMintedCursor runs BigInt(part) on a cursor of arbitrary length. `since` is caller-supplied through parley_fetch_recent (packages/bridge-core/src/transport/tools.ts:93 declares it as a bare z.string() with no .max()), and BigInt's decimal parse is superlinear, so one tool call blocks the single-threaded MCP process — including every other session's push loop and every in-flight long poll — for as long as the caller cares to pay for.
failure: Measured through the real plugin against a live Redis: fetchRecent({topic, since: '9'.repeat(4_000_000)}) -> 782ms of synchronous event-loop stall before the (correct) malformed-cursor rejection. Scaling is superlinear: 1e5 digits 8ms, 1e6 142ms, 4e6 782ms, so a ~40MB `since` costs roughly 10-15s of full-process stall for one request. The regex /^\d+(-\d+)?$/ runs first and is linear, so the cost is entirely the BigInt.
remediation: Refuse an over-long cursor before parsing it: in assertMintedCursor, treat `since.length > MAX_CURSOR_CHARS` as malformed and throw the existing labelled error. A stream entry id is at most 20+1+20 = 41 characters, so any generous constant (say 128) is far above anything Redis can mint while cutting the parse cost to O(1).
testUpgrade: The class is "an untrusted, caller-controlled string reaching a superlinear parser with no length bound". Add a parameterized bound case to live-stream.test.ts's cursor-provenance table rather than a single row: generate `since` at lengths [41, MAX_CURSOR_CHARS, MAX_CURSOR_CHARS+1, 1e4, 1e6] in both the all-digit and the <ms>-<seq> shapes, assert every over-bound one rejects with the labelled malformed-cursor error, and assert wall-clock cost stays under a fixed ceiling (e.g. 50ms) for the largest — a bound with no timing assertion is satisfied by a slow implementation. The same generator should be run against every other backend's cursor validator, since `since` is caller-supplied at the same core tool for all of them.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The existing pluginError(...) throw inside assertMintedCursor and its message text, which live-stream.test.ts's `foreign` table matches with new RegExp('parley-redis: malformed cursor .* for topic ' + t) — a length-rejected cursor must take that same throw, not a new one, or those rows break.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A cursor longer than the bound that today parses to a small number — concretely '0'.repeat(200) + '1-0', which BigInt reads as 1-0 and the plugin currently accepts as a live cursor. This is a real behaviour change and it is the sharp edge of this fix: live-stream.test.ts deliberately grades a leading-zero SPELLING axis (respell(id, 3, 3)), so the bound must be comfortably above 47 characters or that whole axis goes red. 128 clears it; anything at or near 41 does not.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none at a bound of 128 — I checked live-stream.test.ts's spellings array (max padding 3 zeros per component, so max 47 chars) and its foreign table (longest row is '18446744073709551616-18446744073709551616', 41 chars), and subscribe-hardening's long-poll cursors ('500-0','1-0','123','999999998-4'). I did NOT apply and re-run this one.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the stall for this backend only. If applied while core's z.string() stays unbounded, the same megabyte still crosses the JSON-RPC boundary and is still allocated and regex-scanned — the residual cost is linear, not superlinear, and every other backend's cursor validator remains exposed on its own terms.

summary: The beyond-high-water self-heal returns messages strictly OLDER than `since` and a nextCursor BELOW `since`. seam.ts:116 states the opposite without qualification ("Returns messages strictly after `since`"), and the frozen conformance suite has no clause for it — packages/conformance/src/clauses.ts lists 21 clauses and none covers a stale cursor. At least four shipped backends (redis, sqlite, nats, telegram) implement this same heal privately, each graded only by its own package's table, so the shared suite certifies a backend that omits the heal (wedging a topic forever) exactly as readily as one that has it.
failure: fetchRecent({topic:'t', since:'<tail+1h>-0'}) on a topic whose stream holds ['one','two'] returns {messages:[one,two], nextCursor:<cursor of two>} — two messages strictly BEFORE the `since` the caller asked to read after, and a nextCursor lower than the one they passed in. A core (or an embedder) written against seam.ts's stated contract has no reason to expect either. The seam and the conformance suite are silent, so no cross-backend grade exists.
remediation: This is not a bridge-redis change — the seam is what is wrong, and per CLAUDE.md prime directive 2 it must be surfaced rather than absorbed. Declare the arm in seam.ts's fetchRecent doc the way the absent-topic arm is already declared, add a staleCursorBehaviour: 'replays-recent-window' | 'echoes' capability to ConformanceContext (required, with the stricter value as the default, matching the existing absentTopicBehaviour pattern), and add one conformance case + one CLAUSES entry: mint a cursor past what the backend can ever have minted, assert the page is never both empty AND nextCursor === since.
testUpgrade: The class is "a behaviour every backend must share, graded only by each backend's private table". The durable guard is the conformance clause above, driven off a context-supplied staleCursor(topic) minter so each backend expresses "a cursor past my high-water mark" in its own id space (redis: tail ms + 1h; sqlite: max rowid + 1; nats: seq + 1). Grade the invariant, not the outcome: messages.length > 0 || nextCursor !== since, plus "the returned cursor is live" (post once more, re-fetch from it, get exactly the new message). bridge-redis's own live-stream.test.ts table is already written this way and is the model — it is just not shared.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: packages/conformance/src/factory.ts's CONTEXT_FIELDS runtime validator, which is what makes a capability field REQUIRED (vitest transpiles without typechecking, so a missing field would otherwise silently delete cases), and clauses.ts's CLAUSES membership check, which is what makes deleting the new clause a failure.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: Nothing at runtime in bridge-redis; the plugin's behaviour is unchanged. It newly accepts, as CONFORMANT, a backend that declares staleCursorBehaviour: 'echoes' and is then graded on the echo arm instead of the replay arm.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Every backend whose conformance context omits the new field fails assertConformanceContext at fixture time — that is the intended failure, but it means the change cannot land in bridge-redis alone; all 11 backends' factories must be updated in the same commit or their suites go red.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: packages/conformance's own suite-shape/CLAUSES membership tests, which pin CLAUSES.length and CONTEXT_FIELDS keys by value — they must be updated with the new clause and field. Every backend's conformance.test.ts makeContext() would fail the field validator until updated. I did not run this; it is derived from reading factory.ts and clauses.ts.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the grading gap only. If applied while a backend's heal is still wrong, the new clause is what catches it — but nothing here changes redis's behaviour, and a core or embedder that assumed monotonic nextCursor still has to be audited separately (core's catchUpTopic at engine/catchup.ts:71 already tolerates a lower cursor, because it stops on messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since rather than on a comparison).

summary: open() calls tearDown(), which bumps the generation and kills every subscribe read loop. The plugin never re-establishes those subscriptions and writes nothing to stderr. Every other way live delivery dies is announced — a permanent refusal writes STOPPED, a sustained transient fault writes DEGRADED, and diagnostics.ts justifies both with "a live path which can no longer deliver does not look identical to a quiet topic". A second connect() produces exactly that state and is the one path that says nothing.
failure: await p.connect(cfg); await p.subscribe(t, h); await p.connect(cfg); — from here on h is never called again for any message posted to t, subscribe() long since resolved, post/fetchRecent keep working, and no line is written anywhere. subscribe-hardening.test.ts's 'connect() re-baselining the generation' rows cement this silence (they assert only that no further reads are issued and no timer is armed). README.md documents STOPPED and DEGRADED and never mentions reconnect at all.
remediation: Make the loss loud rather than silent. Either (a) have tearDown() report, when it is being called from open() rather than from disconnect() and at least one subscribe reader was live, one line naming the topics whose live delivery ended; or (b) fail fast — have connect() reject when the plugin is already connected and holds live subscriptions, since core (transport/stdio-bridge.ts:67) connects exactly once and nothing in this repo needs a hot reconnect. (b) is the smaller change and is more in keeping with "no silent no-ops".
testUpgrade: The class is "a lifecycle call that silently ends a capability the plugin announces the end of on every other path". Parameterize a table over (way live delivery ends) x (what must be observable): rows = [permanent refusal, sustained transient fault, disconnect(), connect() re-baseline, handler that throws], and assert for each row whether a diagnostic line is owed and whether the handler stops. disconnect() is the negative control (silence is correct there); today the connect() row is the only one that is both silent and unexpected. Written this way, a future lifecycle path added to tearDown's callers is pulled into the table rather than escaping it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: this.readers and the generation counter in index.ts. Note tearDown() does NOT currently know which readers are subscribe readers vs long-poll readers — the readers array holds both and blockingReaders is only a count — so option (a) needs a per-reader tag that does not exist today.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Under option (b): a second connect() on a plugin that already holds subscriptions now rejects. That is a behaviour change an embedder could be relying on for hot config reload.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Option (b) would break, by name: live-connections.test.ts 'connect·subscribe·connect·disconnect returns every socket', 'connect ∥ subscribe' and 'connect·(connect ∥ fetchRecent(blocking))', and subscribe-hardening.test.ts's four 'connect() re-baselining the generation after ...' rows plus 'does not revive a prior loop after disconnect()/connect()'. That is a substantial ratchet to move, and those rows encode a real invariant (no orphaned sockets across a re-connect) that must survive whatever replaces them. Option (a) breaks none of them that I can see — subscribe-hardening's stderr spy rows assert diagnosed === (kind==='permanent') before their finally calls disconnect(), and the re-baseline rows assert only read counts and timer counts — but I did not apply and run either option.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Option (a) fixes the observability and leaves the capability lost — an operator learns about it, live push still needs a restart. Option (b) fixes it by refusing to enter the state at all. Neither restores the subscriptions; re-subscribing across a reconnect would be a third, larger change and would need the topic->handler map the plugin deliberately does not keep.

summary: Three comments direct a reader to test files that are not in the package. config-fixtures.ts:2 and failure-modes.test.ts:40 and :348 all name live-failure-modes.test.ts; support.ts:13 names endpoint-hygiene.test.ts. Neither file exists anywhere in the repo (grep across packages/ finds only these four mentions). Each is load-bearing prose: config-fixtures.ts claims the missing file is what asserts "a rejected row never tears a live connection down", and support.ts cites the missing file as the enforcement behind its endpoint-minting rule.
failure: A maintainer following config-fixtures.ts's instruction — "Keep one copy, so that the two files cannot drift and leave a knob rejected in one and unguarded in the other" — goes looking for live-failure-modes.test.ts to check the second consumer, finds nothing, and concludes the second guard was deleted. It was not: the assertion lives in live-config.test.ts's 'a rejected connect() must not destroy a live one' block, and the endpoint rule lives in test-hygiene.test.ts.
